adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Equal-priority full providers are now silently chosen by ServiceLoader order, so a default provider can win over FIPS and bypass the intended cryptographic boundary

authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — First-use initialization can permanently install the partial fallback globally even when client construction later fails, cascading UnsupportedOperationException failures into unrelated crypto consumers

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue: CryptoIntegration.init() is called in the static create() method at line 95, which sets a global singleton crypto provider. Looking at CryptoIntegration.java, the init() method uses detectProvider() which now selects the highest-order provider. The AuthzClientCryptoProvider has order=100 while other providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) have order=200. So AuthzClientCryptoProvider would only be selected if no other provider is available. However, the concern is valid: if AuthzClient.create() is called first in an application before other crypto providers are loaded, and if the AuthzClientCryptoProvider gets installed (being the only one available at that moment), it will remain globally installed. This partial provider throws UnsupportedOperationException for many operations, which could cause failures in other parts of the application that later try to use crypto operations. The initialization happens regardless of whether the AuthzClient construction succeeds.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:109 — The converter copies only signLength bytes and ignores an attacker-controlled suffix, so an otherwise valid ECDSA signature still verifies after arbitrary bytes are appended

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that asn1derToConcatenatedRS ignores trailing bytes, allowing signature malleability. However, examining the code at line 109 (the asn1derToConcatenatedRS method), it properly parses the ASN.1 DER structure using ASN1Decoder.readSequence() which reads the exact sequence length specified in the DER encoding. The method then extracts exactly two integers (r and s) from the sequence. If there were extra bytes, the ASN1Decoder would either fail during parsing or they would be outside the parsed sequence structure. The method doesn't simply copy signLength bytes from input - it properly decodes the ASN.1 structure. This is a signature format conversion utility, not signature verification itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:55 — Sequence parsing neither confines children to the declared length nor requires input exhaustion, silently canonicalizing DER with truncated container lengths or trailing data

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the readSequence() method in ASN1Decoder.java (lines 49-60), the code reads the declared length but then uses a while loop that decrements length by the size of each child element read. However, the issue is that it subtracts `bytes.length` (the full encoded child including tag/length) from the remaining length, but there's no validation that: 1) children don't extend beyond the declared sequence length, 2) the input is fully consumed after parsing. The readNext() method reads arbitrary bytes without bounds checking against the parent sequence's declared length. This could allow malformed DER with truncated lengths or trailing data to be silently accepted, which is a correctness/security concern for ASN1 parsing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Equal provider orders now resolve by unspecified ServiceLoader iteration order, so coexisting default, FIPS, or custom providers can select different crypto backends instead of failing deterministically

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that when multiple CryptoProviders have the same order() value, the selection depends on ServiceLoader iteration order, which is not deterministic. Looking at the diff, the code sorts by order().reversed() (line 57) and takes the first element (line 66). The new AuthzClientCryptoProvider has order() 100, while DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all have order() 200. So in practice, the higher-order providers would be selected over AuthzClientCryptoProvider. However, if two providers with order() 200 are on the classpath (e.g., default and FIPS), the selection between them would indeed be non-deterministic. This is a valid architectural concern about the change, though not a bug since the intended use case (AuthzClient with its lower-priority provider) works correctly.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — Using AuthzClient's defining loader ignores caller-visible CryptoProvider services exposed only through the context class loader and can lock the process onto the partial fallback provider

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to a real architectural concern in the diff. At line 95, CryptoIntegration.init() is called with AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader(), which is the classloader that loaded the AuthzClient class itself. This means ServiceLoader will only find CryptoProvider implementations visible to that specific classloader, not those that might be available through Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader(). In environments where the caller has additional CryptoProvider implementations on their context classloader (common in application servers, OSGi, etc.), these would be ignored, potentially causing the fallback AuthzClientCryptoProvider (with order=100) to be selected instead of a more complete provider (order=200). This is a legitimate scope/architecture concern introduced by this change, though not strictly a bug since the code will function with the fallback provider.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/resources/META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider:20 — Registering a provider that throws UnsupportedOperationException for most mandatory CryptoProvider methods lets unrelated consumers receive an SPI implementation that violates the advertised contract

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a legitimate architectural concern. The diff shows AuthzClientCryptoProvider is registered as a CryptoProvider via SPI (META-INF/services), but most methods throw UnsupportedOperationException. The CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() method (modified in this diff) now selects providers by order() - AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns 100 while others return 200, so it would only be selected if no other provider is available. However, if the authz-client jar is on the classpath without a full crypto provider, consumers calling methods like getCertificateUtils() or getPemUtils() would get UnsupportedOperationException. This is a valid design/architecture concern about partial SPI implementations, though the order mechanism mitigates it when proper providers are present.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — Making order() abstract breaks every out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation instead of preserving the SPI boundary with a default priority

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that CryptoProvider.java adds a new method `int order();` to the interface without a default implementation. This is a breaking change for any external implementations of CryptoProvider that exist outside this codebase. While the diff shows that internal implementations (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider, AuthzClientCryptoProvider) all add the order() method, any third-party implementations would fail to compile after this change. The finding correctly identifies that adding a default method (e.g., `default int order() { return 0; }`) would preserve backward compatibility.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — Initializing the process-global CryptoIntegration singleton from AuthzClient's classloader makes the first client construction permanently choose a provider for unrelated crypto consumers

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real architectural concern. The diff shows CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) is called in AuthzClient.create(), and looking at CryptoIntegration.java, the init method uses a singleton pattern (cryptoProvider field) that gets set once and persists. The detectProvider method uses the passed classLoader to load CryptoProvider implementations via ServiceLoader. This means the first AuthzClient.create() call will permanently set the global crypto provider based on AuthzClient's classloader, which could affect other unrelated crypto consumers in the same JVM. This is a legitimate scope/architecture concern introduced by the change, though not strictly a bug since it may work correctly in many scenarios.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:58 — This partial implementation is exposed as a full CryptoProvider despite most capabilities throwing UnsupportedOperationException, forcing callers to know which implementation was selected

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that AuthzClientCryptoProvider implements CryptoProvider but throws UnsupportedOperationException for most methods. However, this is an intentional design choice - the class is specifically designed as a minimal crypto provider for the authz-client module (as stated in the javadoc 'Simple crypto provider to be used with the authz-client'). The order() method returns 100, which is lower than the 200 returned by other providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider), meaning this provider will only be selected when no other provider is available. The CryptoIntegration changes show providers are sorted by order in descending order, so higher-order providers take precedence. This is a legitimate architectural concern about partial implementations, but it's a deliberate design decision rather than a bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Provider precedence is distributed as magic numbers and all full providers tie at 200, so selection remains dependent on ServiceLoader discovery order

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that all full crypto providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) return order() = 200, while only AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns 100. This means when multiple full providers are on the classpath, they all tie at 200 and selection depends on ServiceLoader discovery order, which is non-deterministic. The diff shows the new ordering mechanism in CryptoIntegration.java line 57 sorts by order() reversed, but the magic number approach with ties doesn't fully solve the multi-provider ambiguity problem. This is a legitimate architectural concern about the design introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:114 — These two standalone ASN1Encoder writes discard their results and are dead code that obscures the actual encoding path

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:33 — A 300-line general-purpose ASN.1 encoder/decoder abstraction is maintained for one fixed two-integer ECDSA shape and should be narrowed to that format

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that ASN1Decoder and ASN1Encoder (combined ~300 lines) are general-purpose ASN.1 implementations but are only used for the specific case of encoding/decoding two-integer ECDSA signatures. The diff shows these classes have methods like readSequence(), readInteger(), readTag(), readTagNumber(), readLength() etc. that handle general ASN.1 parsing, but the actual usage in AuthzClientCryptoProvider only reads a sequence of exactly 2 integers. This is a valid architectural concern - the code could be simplified to only handle the specific ECDSA signature format rather than maintaining a general ASN.1 library. However, this is a design/scope concern rather than a bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:63 — getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider rather than BouncyCastle, so dependent cryptographic initialization or operations can fail under this provider

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that getBouncyCastleProvider() returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider() which is NOT BouncyCastle - it's whatever the default keystore provider is. However, looking at the context, this is a simplified crypto provider for authz-client that explicitly throws UnsupportedOperationException for most methods. The class is designed as a minimal implementation (order=100, lower than the full providers at order=200) that only supports specific operations like ECDSA. The getBouncyCastleProvider() implementation is questionable but may be intentional for this limited use case. This is a legitimate design/architecture concern worth discussing, but not necessarily a bug since the provider is designed to be overridden by more complete providers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:109 — Missing an exact signature-length check lets valid ECDSA JWT signatures remain valid after attacker-controlled bytes are appended, enabling token-identity and replay-control bypasses.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims there's a missing signature-length check that allows appending bytes to ECDSA signatures. Looking at the actual code in asn1derToConcatenatedRS at line 109+, the method reads exactly 2 elements from the ASN1 sequence, extracts the r and s BigIntegers, converts them to fixed-length byte arrays using integerToBytes (which enforces exact length), and creates a concatenated signature of exactly signLength bytes. The integerToBytes method properly handles both truncation and padding to ensure exact length. The ASN1Decoder reads the sequence structure properly. There's no vulnerability where appended bytes would be accepted - the ASN1 parsing reads exactly what's specified in the length fields, and the output is always exactly signLength bytes. This is a false positive.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Equal-priority providers are silently selected by classpath discovery order, so deployments containing both the default and FIPS providers can unintentionally run outside the required FIPS cryptographic boundary.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims equal-priority providers are silently selected by classpath order, but the diff shows that DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all have order() returning 200, while AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns 100. The code sorts by order in descending order (reversed()), so higher-order providers (200) are preferred over lower-order ones (100). The FIPS provider and default provider have the same priority (200), but this is existing behavior - the diff doesn't introduce this issue. The diff actually improves the situation by adding ordering capability and logging which providers are ignored. The finding mischaracterizes what the diff does.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:56 — The test only round-trips through the same codec, so invalid DER can pass without verification by JCA or independent vectors.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a limitation in the test design. Looking at the test in ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java (lines 48-58), it signs data with JCA, converts the DER signature to concatenated RS format, then converts back to DER, and only verifies that the two concatenated RS arrays match (rsConcat == rsConcat2). The test never verifies the final DER signature against JCA's Signature.verify(), meaning a buggy encoder could produce invalid DER that still round-trips through the same buggy decoder. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added cryptographic code - the ASN1Encoder/ASN1Decoder implementations should be validated against an independent reference (JCA verification) rather than just self-consistency.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 — All three cases reuse an uninitialized default EC generator, so ES384 and ES512 do not reliably exercise P-384/P-521 scalar widths or ES512 long-form DER lengths.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test uses a single KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() without specifying curve parameters, which defaults to a single curve (typically P-256). This means testES384() and testES512() don't actually test with P-384 and P-521 keys respectively - they all use the same default curve. While the conversion logic is still exercised with different signLength parameters, the test doesn't verify the code works correctly with actual signatures from different curve sizes. This is a legitimate test coverage gap for newly added cryptographic code, though not a bug in the production code itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:56 — No test covers the new multi-provider ServiceLoader ordering, leaving priority direction and equal-priority selection regressions undetected.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a new test file ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java was added, but it only tests the ECDSA crypto provider functionality. The CryptoIntegration.java changes at line 56 introduce new multi-provider ordering logic using Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed(), but there is no test in the diff that verifies this ordering behavior works correctly. This is a valid concern - the new ordering logic is nontrivial (sorting by order() in descending order, selecting highest priority) and could have regressions if the sorting direction or tie-breaking behavior changes. The finding correctly identifies missing test coverage for specific new logic in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — The test constructs the provider directly and never creates an AuthzClient, so the service registration and automatic initialization path are untested.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test file ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java directly instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider rather than going through AuthzClient.create(), which would trigger CryptoIntegration.init() and load the provider via ServiceLoader. This means the service registration in META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider and the automatic initialization path in AuthzClient.create() are not exercised by the test. This is a valid test coverage concern for the new functionality.
